hints: Focus on what the question is really asking, forces based only on temporary dipoles means London dispersion forces with no permanent dipole or hydrogen bonding.
Check each liquid for polarity, only a non-polar molecule with no O-H, N-H or permanent dipole will qualify.
Compare the diatomic halogen with the three polar molecules containing O-H or H-Cl bonds to see which one is left with dispersion forces alone.
walkthrough:
**Recall what temporary dipole forces mean**

Great start, let's get the language clear. Forces based on temporary dipoles are London dispersion forces, also called induced dipole-dipole forces.

Every molecule has them, but the question asks for a liquid that has ONLY these forces and nothing stronger.

**Decide when stronger forces appear**

If a molecule is polar, it also has permanent dipole-dipole forces. If it has H attached to O or N, it also has hydrogen bonding.

So we are looking for a non-polar molecule with no permanent dipole and no hydrogen bonding.

**Test each liquid**

$\text{Br}_2$ is a non-polar diatomic molecule, the two identical Br atoms share electrons equally, so there is no permanent dipole.

$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ are all polar. Ethanol and water have $\text{O-H}$ groups so they hydrogen bond, and $\text{HCl}$ has a permanent dipole.

Therefore only liquid bromine has London dispersion forces alone between its particles.

options.A: Correct, bromine exists as non-polar $\text{Br}_2$ molecules. With equal sharing of electrons there is no permanent dipole and no hydrogen bonding, so the only intermolecular forces are London dispersion forces from temporary dipoles.
options.B: Incorrect. Ethanol, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, contains an O-H group so it forms hydrogen bonds in addition to permanent dipole-dipole forces and London forces. Students who choose this may forget that any O-H group brings hydrogen bonding.
options.C: Incorrect. Hydrogen chloride, $\text{HCl}$, is polar because Cl is much more electronegative than H, so it has permanent dipole-dipole forces as well as London forces. The trap is thinking a small simple molecule has only temporary dipoles.
options.D: Incorrect. Water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, is polar and has two O-H bonds, so it forms strong hydrogen bonds plus permanent dipole-dipole forces and London forces. It is a classic example of hydrogen bonding, not dispersion only.
